future_direction: Investigating language adaptation techniques to enable models to perform tasks in a more language-agnostic manner.
Exploring the role that each architecture component plays in alternative domains to enhance explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored methods for updating and modifying factual knowledge in large language models, often focusing on specific multi-layer perceptron blocks. This study expands on this work by examining the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and delving into the role of attention mechanisms in this process. Drawing from the insights gained, we propose Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers (MEMAT), a method that achieves significant improvements in all metrics while requiring minimal parameter modifications. MEMAT delivers a remarkable 10% increase in magnitude metrics, benefits languages not included in the training data and also demonstrates a high degree of portability. Our code and data are at https://github.com/dtamayo-nlp/MEMAT.

papers.title: Extractive Structures Learned in Pretraining Enable Generalization on Finetuned Facts
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models generalize to implications of facts they are finetuned on, and what mechanisms (extractive structures) enable this out-of-context reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the extractive structures framework to explain how language models generalize to implications of finetuned facts, and empirically validates two predictions of how these structures are learned: a data ordering effect and a weight grafting effect.
papers.conclusion: The extractive structures framework provides a mechanism for understanding out-of-context reasoning, and the empirical findings (data ordering and weight grafting) support the hypothesis that these structures are learned during pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Extractive structures (informative, upstream, downstream components) are identified in the OLMo-7b model for two-hop reasoning tasks, with MLPs and attention heads playing specific roles.
Fact learning occurs in both early and late layers, with early layers enabling first-hop generalization and late layers enabling second-hop generalization.
A data ordering effect is observed: extractive structures are learned only if facts precede their implications during training.
Weight grafting (weight-space arithmetic) can transfer newly learned extractive structures to predict counterfactual implications.
Attention heads, not just MLPs, can store factual information as weight changes.
papers.limitation: The nature of an alternative mechanism hinted at in the data ordering experiments remains unclear, and the finetuning process's dependence on hyperparameters and the pretrained model is not fully characterized.
future_direction: Developing an underlying theory of generalization that captures the dynamical nature of optimization.
Applying the extractive structures framework more broadly to understand and ground out-of-context generalization beyond two-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) can generalize to implications of facts that they are finetuned on. For example, if finetuned on ``John Doe lives in Tokyo," LMs can correctly answer ``What language do the people in John Doe's city speak?'' with ``Japanese''. However, little is known about the mechanisms that enable this generalization or how they are learned during pretraining. We introduce extractive structures as a framework for describing how components in LMs (e.g., MLPs or attention heads) coordinate to enable this generalization. The structures consist of informative components that store training facts as weight changes, and upstream and downstream extractive components that query and process the stored information to produce the correct implication. We hypothesize that extractive structures are learned during pretraining when encountering implications of previously known facts. This yields two predictions: a data ordering effect where extractive structures can be learned only if facts precede their implications, and a weight grafting effect where extractive structures can be transferred to predict counterfactual implications. We empirically demonstrate these phenomena in the OLMo-7b, Llama 3-8b, Gemma 2-9b, and Qwen 2-7b models. Of independent interest, our results also indicate that fact learning can occur at both early and late layers, which lead to different forms of generalization.

papers.title: The Mechanics of Conceptual Interpretation in GPT Models: Interpretative Insights
papers.research_question: What are the observable representation patterns that characterise conceptual interpretation within language models? Can we localise specialised representational patterns to derive an interpretation model within language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces concept editing, a variation of knowledge editing, to uncover conceptualization mechanisms in LLMs, and through analysis of MLP, MHA, and hidden states, reveals distinct patterns of semantic processing.
papers.conclusion: The work elucidates how transformer models process semantic information through distinct component interactions, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
MLP layers employ key-value retrieval and context-dependent processing, focusing on specific lexical and semantic features.
MHA layers show distributed nature with higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration.
Hidden states emphasize the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process, indicating gradual information building.
Concept interpretation involves a collaborative process among model components, with compositionality being critical.
Patterns are consistent across languages (English and Spanish) and across alternative definitions, indicating robust processing strategies.
papers.abstract: Locating and editing knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their accuracy, safety, and inference rationale. We introduce ``concept editing'', an innovative variation of knowledge editing that uncovers conceptualisation mechanisms within these models. Using the reverse dictionary task, inference tracing, and input abstraction, we analyse the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Multi-Head Attention (MHA), and hidden state components of transformer models. Our results reveal distinct patterns: MLP layers employ key-value retrieval mechanism and context-dependent processing, which are highly associated with relative input tokens. MHA layers demonstrate a distributed nature with significant higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration. Hidden states emphasise the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process. We observe evidence of gradual information building and distributed representation. These observations elucidate how transformer models process semantic information, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques. Our work highlights the complex, layered nature of semantic processing in LLMs and the challenges of isolating and modifying specific concepts within these models.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Learn Concepts During Continual Pre-Training?
papers.research_question: How do large language models acquire, retain, and forget concepts during continual pretraining? Specifically, how do internal concept representations correlate with concept acquisition and forgetting, and how do they relate to interference and synergy among multiple concepts and knowledge types during joint training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a circuit-level analysis of concept learning in LLMs during continual pre-training, revealing that concept circuits provide signals for learning and forgetting dynamics, and show patterns like stage-wise temporal changes and interference/synergy effects.
papers.conclusion: The work offers a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and informs the design of more interpretable and robust concept-aware training strategies for LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Concept circuits provide a non-trivial, statistically significant signal of concept learning and forgetting.
Concept circuits exhibit a stage-wise temporal pattern during continual pretraining, with an early increase followed by gradual decrease and stabilization.
Concepts with larger learning gains tend to exhibit greater forgetting under subsequent training.
Semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones.
Conceptual knowledge differs in transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others.
papers.limitation:
Limited model scale, focusing only on GPT-2 Large and LLaMA-3.2-1B, not larger models.
Exploration of actionable training strategies is left for future work.
future_direction: Extending analysis to larger-scale models.
Exploring circuit-aware training effort allocation and interference-aware data scheduling.
papers.abstract: Human beings primarily understand the world through concepts (e.g., dog), abstract mental representations that structure perception, reasoning, and learning. However, how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and forget such concepts during continual pretraining remains poorly understood. In this work, we study how individual concepts are acquired and forgotten, as well as how multiple concepts interact through interference and synergy. We link these behavioral dynamics to LLMs' internal Concept Circuits, computational subgraphs associated with specific concepts, and incorporate Graph Metrics to characterize circuit structure. Our analysis reveals: (1) LLMs concept circuits provide a non-trivial, statistically significant signal of concept learning and forgetting; (2) Concept circuits exhibit a stage-wise temporal pattern during continual pretraining, with an early increase followed by gradual decrease and stabilization; (3) concepts with larger learning gains tend to exhibit greater forgetting under subsequent training; (4) semantically similar concepts induce stronger interference than weakly related ones; (5) conceptual knowledge differs in their transferability, with some significantly facilitating the learning of others. Together, our findings offer a circuit-level view of concept learning dynamics and inform the design of more interpretable and robust concept-aware training strategies for LLMs.

papers.title: Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that knowledge-conflicting facts are most enduring in language models and proposes a sparsification method to erase them while preserving task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers that knowledge-conflicting facts endure for many updates and cause inappropriate priming, and shows that their impact can be mitigated via multi-step sparse updates while preserving main task training.
papers.key_findings:
Facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while mundane and scrambled facts are forgotten more rapidly.
Knowledge-conflicting facts can prime how the model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts.
There is a sweet spot in fact novelty (between consistency and randomness) for memory durability.
The impact of knowledge-conflicting facts can be erased by multi-step sparse updates while preserving task performance.
future_direction: Extend the Outlandish dataset further
papers.abstract: What happens when a new piece of knowledge is introduced into the training data and how long does it last while a large language model (LM) continues to train? We investigate this question by injecting facts into LMs from a new probing dataset, "Outlandish", which is designed to permit the testing of a spectrum of different fact types. When studying how robust these memories are, there appears to be a sweet spot in the spectrum of fact novelty between consistency with world knowledge and total randomness, where the injected memory is the most enduring. Specifically we show that facts that conflict with common knowledge are remembered for tens of thousands of training steps, while prompts not conflicting with common knowledge (mundane), as well as scrambled prompts (randomly jumbled) are both forgotten much more rapidly. Further, knowledge-conflicting facts can "prime'' how the language model hallucinates on logically unrelated prompts, showing their propensity for non-target generalization, while both mundane and randomly jumbled facts prime significantly less. Finally, we show that impacts of knowledge-conflicting facts in LMs, though they can be long lasting, can be largely erased by novel application of multi-step sparse updates, even while the training ability of the model is preserved. As such, this very simple procedure has direct implications for mitigating the effects of data poisoning in training.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Where Knowledge Collides: A Mechanistic Study of Intra-Memory Knowledge Conflict in Language Models
papers.research_question: Which internal components of language models are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training data, and can noisy or incorrect information be selectively suppressed during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mechanistic interpretability framework to localize and intervene on conflicting knowledge encoded in language models, showing that attention components in later layers play a key role in encoding and resolving such conflicts.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a mechanistic interpretability framework to study intra-memory knowledge conflict, demonstrating that logit inspection, activation patching, and cross-model patching can localize and intervene on conflicting internal representations at inference time.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting training data reduces model confidence and introduces confusion in later layers.
Attention components in later layers dominate in shaping factual responses and encoding conflicting knowledge.
Activation patching can steer model generation toward accurate outputs, with success rates varying across models (up to 22% for GPT-2 XL and 70% for Qwen3-4B).
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) improves steering success and reduces noise compared to standard activation patching, especially for certain conflict attributes.
Findings generalize across different model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B), though intervention effectiveness varies.
papers.limitation:
Limited set of conflict types and restriction to a 1:1 ratio of conflicting information per entity.
Results are presented on a limited set of model architectures (GPT-2 XL and Qwen3-4B).
The underlying factors that drive the model's preference for one conflicting fact over another are not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend these methods to knowledge editing and robust information tracing across prompts and model variants.
Include more conflict types and multiple conflicting information per entity.
Evaluate across additional model families.
papers.abstract: In language models (LMs), intra-memory knowledge conflict largely arises when inconsistent information about the same event is encoded within the model's parametric knowledge. While prior work has primarily focused on resolving conflicts between a model's internal knowledge and external resources through approaches such as fine-tuning or knowledge editing, the problem of localizing conflicts that originate during pre-training within the model's internal representations remain unexplored. In this work, we design a framework based on mechanistic interpretability methods to identify where and how conflicting knowledge from the pre-training data is encoded within LMs. Our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence that specific internal components of a language model are responsible for encoding conflicting knowledge from pre-training, and we demonstrate how mechanistic interpretability methods can be leveraged to causally intervene in and control conflicting knowledge at inference time.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: Factual Probing Is [MASK]: Learning vs. Learning to Recall
papers.research_question: Can we interpret factual probing results as a lower bound on the factual information encoded in a language model, or do prompt-search methods learn from the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces OPTI PROMPT, a continuous prompt optimization method that improves factual probing accuracy, and shows that optimized prompts can exploit regularities in training data, complicating the interpretation of probing results.
papers.conclusion: OPTI PROMPT is an effective method for factual probing, but data-driven prompt optimization can exploit training data regularities, making it challenging to interpret probing results as a pure lower bound on model knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
OPTI PROMPT improves top-1 accuracy on the LAMA benchmark by 6.4% over previous methods.
Training data for factual probing contains regularities (e.g., class priors, lexical correlations) that can be exploited by prompt optimization methods.
Optimized prompts can predict facts even when probing randomly initialized models, indicating they learn from training data rather than solely eliciting stored knowledge.
Partitioning test facts into 'easy' (predictable from training data) and 'hard' subsets reveals that OPTI PROMPT improves on both, suggesting it is better at learning from data and eliciting facts from the language model.
Continuous prompt optimization is more efficient and effective than discrete token search, but requires white-box model access.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to determine whether a prediction comes from the language model's stored knowledge or from patterns learned from the training data during prompt optimization.
Gradient-based prompt optimization methods like OPTI PROMPT require white-box access to the model, limiting their use with API-based large models.
future_direction: Develop techniques for attributing predictions to specific training instances to better understand the source of factual knowledge.
Pursue more mechanistic explanations for how language models learn and represent factual information, beyond prompt-based probing.
papers.abstract: demonstrated that it is possible to retrieve world facts from a pretrained language model by expressing them as cloze-style prompts and interpret the model's prediction accuracy as a lower bound on the amount of factual information it encodes. Subsequent work has attempted to tighten the estimate by searching for better prompts, using a disjoint set of facts as training data. In this work, we make two complementary contributions to better understand these factual probing techniques. First, we propose OPTIPROMPT, a novel and efficient method which directly optimizes in continuous embedding space. We find this simple method is able to predict an additional 6.4% of facts in the LAMA benchmark. Second, we raise a more important question: Can we really interpret these probing results as a lower bound? Is it possible that these prompt-search methods learn from the training data too? We find, somewhat surprisingly, that the training data used by these methods contains certain regularities of the underlying fact distribution, and all the existing prompt methods, including ours, are able to exploit them for better fact prediction. We conduct a set of control experiments to disentangle "learning" from "learning to recall", providing a more detailed picture of what different prompts can reveal about pre-trained language models.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: Finding patterns in Knowledge Attribution for Transformers
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how factual, relational, and grammatical knowledge are attributed to neurons in different layers of a transformer model, and whether multilingual facts share the same neurons.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that factual knowledge is attributed to middle and higher layers, relational knowledge to middle layers, and grammatical knowledge is more dispersed. It also shows that multilingual facts share neurons, indicating a common representation space.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents patterns on the location of different types of knowledge in transformer networks and their interactions across languages using the Knowledge Neurons attribution technique.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge is attributed to middle and higher layers (>=6).
Relational knowledge is mostly in layers 6-9, and factual knowledge is refined in layers 10-12.
The same neurons are activated for facts in different languages, indicating a common representation space.
Grammatical knowledge is more dispersed across layers compared to factual knowledge.
The number of attractors in grammatical tasks affects attribution scores and variation.
future_direction: Explore other attribution techniques
Apply analysis to other language models like GPT
papers.abstract: We analyze the Knowledge Neurons framework for the attribution of factual and relational knowledge to particular neurons in the transformer network. We use a 12-layer multi-lingual BERT model for our experiments. Our study reveals various interesting phenomena. We observe that mostly factual knowledge can be attributed to middle and higher layers of the network($\ge 6$). Further analysis reveals that the middle layers($6-9$) are mostly responsible for relational information, which is further refined into actual factual knowledge or the "correct answer" in the last few layers($10-12$). Our experiments also show that the model handles prompts in different languages, but representing the same fact, similarly, providing further evidence for effectiveness of multi-lingual pre-training. Applying the attribution scheme for grammatical knowledge, we find that grammatical knowledge is far more dispersed among the neurons than factual knowledge.

papers.title: Transformers Pretrained on Procedural Data Contain Modular Structures for Algorithmic Reasoning
papers.research_question: What properties of pretraining data enable language models to acquire reasoning capabilities? Specifically, what is gained from procedural data, where does the useful knowledge reside in the pretrained models, and how does pretraining improve downstream capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Pretraining transformers on procedural data creates modular, transferable structures in different parts of the architecture (attention and MLP layers), which can be composed to jointly reinforce multiple algorithmic reasoning capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Procedural pretraining creates useful, modular structures in different parts of the transformer architecture, suggesting the possibility of disentangling the acquisition of knowledge from reasoning to improve model robustness and data efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Different forms of procedural data (e.g., k-DYCK, STACK, ECA) significantly improve specific downstream algorithmic reasoning capabilities (e.g., memory recall, arithmetic, sorting).
The beneficial inductive biases from pretraining often reside in specific architectural components, with attention layers being the most consistently transferable carrier of useful structure.
Pretraining creates soft inductive biases in precisely structured weights, not merely through adjusting weight magnitudes, as shown by sensitivity to noise and shuffling perturbations.
The structures induced by multiple pretraining rules are modular and can be composed (e.g., combining attention from one model with MLPs from another) to create an initialization that facilitates fine-tuning on multiple tasks.
future_direction: Understanding why specific forms of procedural data help specific capabilities (e.g., why HAYSTACK benefits from k-DYCK but not its SHUFFLE variant).
Exploring data mixture optimization to balance multiple procedural rules for training generalist LLMs.
Characterizing the resulting structure in pretrained models to directly instantiate it in initial weights, avoiding wasteful expansion of simple rules into millions of training examples.
papers.abstract: Pretraining on large, semantically rich datasets is key for developing language models. Surprisingly, recent studies have shown that even synthetic data, generated procedurally through simple semantic-free algorithms, can yield some of the same benefits as natural language pretraining. It is unclear what specific capabilities such simple synthetic data instils in a model, where these capabilities reside in the architecture, and how they manifest within its weights. In this short paper, we identify several beneficial forms of procedural data, together with specific algorithmic reasoning skills that improve in small transformers. Our core finding is that different procedural rules instil distinct but complementary inductive structures in the model. With extensive ablations and partial-transfer experiments, we discover that these structures reside in different parts of the model. Attention layers often carry the most transferable information, but some pretraining rules impart useful structure to MLP blocks instead. Most interestingly, the structures induced by multiple rules can be composed to jointly reinforce multiple capabilities. These results suggest an exciting possibility of disentangling the acquisition of knowledge from reasoning in language models, with the goal of improving their robustness and data efficiency.

papers.title: The Queen of England is not England's Queen: On the Lack of Factual Coherency in PLMs
papers.research_question: What is the coherency of factual knowledge in Pre-trained Language Models, and how does it vary with different prompts and evidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the concept of coherency for factual knowledge in PLMs, demonstrates that PLMs have low coherency, and finds that including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
papers.conclusion: PLMs have poor coherency in factual knowledge, but evidence paragraphs help. Future work should focus on architectural, data, and interface improvements.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs have low coherency in factual knowledge.
Autoregressive PLMs perform worse than masked PLMs.
Optimized prompts do not improve coherency.
Including evidence paragraphs substantially improves coherency.
Coherency varies significantly with paraphrased prompts.
papers.limitation: For N-1 or N-M relations, it is difficult to exclude every possible answer, and only answers present in LAMA are excluded, which might negatively affect the results.
future_direction: Improve PLMs on architectural level.
Improve PLMs on data level.
Improve pre-training objectives and interface.
papers.abstract: Factual knowledge encoded in Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) enriches their representations and justifies their use as knowledge bases. Previous work has focused on probing PLMs for factual knowledge by measuring how often they can correctly predict an object entity given a subject and a relation, and improving fact retrieval by optimizing the prompts used for querying PLMs. In this work, we consider a complementary aspect, namely the coherency of factual knowledge in PLMs, i.e., how often can PLMs predict the subject entity given its initial prediction of the object entity. This goes beyond evaluating how much PLMs know, and focuses on the internal state of knowledge inside them. Our results indicate that PLMs have low coherency using manually written, optimized and paraphrased prompts, but including an evidence paragraph leads to substantial improvement. This shows that PLMs fail to model inverse relations and need further enhancements to be able to handle retrieving facts from their parameters in a coherent manner, and to be considered as knowledge bases.

papers.title: Give Me the Facts! A Survey on Factual Knowledge Probing in Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: What methods and datasets are used to probe pre-trained language models for factual knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This paper surveys methods and datasets for factual knowledge probing in pre-trained language models, proposes a categorization scheme for probing methods based on adaptations to inputs, models, and outputs, and synthesizes insights about knowledge retention and prompt optimization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing future work directions, including improving probing methods by combining adaptations across multiple dimensions, constructing unbiased and comprehensive datasets, and moving beyond simple correctness counts to more comprehensive evaluation schemes.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge probing methods can be categorized based on how their inputs, outputs, and the probed PLMs are adapted.
A wide variety of datasets exist for factual probing, which can be categorized into general knowledge, domain-specific knowledge, and datasets targeting other aspects like consistency or updating knowledge.
Knowledge retention in PLMs is affected by factors such as model size, pre-training data, and the number of training epochs.
Prompt optimization can improve fact retrieval but may introduce biases, and the choice between using optimized or non-optimized prompts depends on the evaluation goal.
Several obstacles hinder the adoption of PLMs as knowledge bases, including issues with consistency, updating knowledge, and interpretability, though recent methods aim to address these.
papers.limitation:
The corpus construction relied on publications citing Petroni et al. (2019), potentially missing parallel works or works that do not directly cite this seminal paper.
The survey focuses on works about factual knowledge and excludes works on other types of knowledge (e.g., linguistic or commonsense), though methods for those types might be applicable to factual knowledge probing.
future_direction: Improving probing methods by introducing adaptations across two or more dimensions (e.g., optimizing inputs while also debiasing outputs).
Constructing unbiased and comprehensive probing datasets that correspond to the capacity of recently published large PLMs.

Developing comprehensive evaluation schemes that include factors like answer frequency, pre-training corpus creation period, model size, and training epochs, rather than just counting correct answers.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) are trained on vast unlabeled data, rich in world knowledge. This fact has sparked the interest of the community in quantifying the amount of factual knowledge present in PLMs, as this explains their performance on downstream tasks, and potentially justifies their use as knowledge bases. In this work, we survey methods and datasets that are used to probe PLMs for factual knowledge. Our contributions are: (1) We propose a categorization scheme for factual probing methods that is based on how their inputs, outputs and the probed PLMs are adapted; (2) We provide an overview of the datasets used for factual probing; (3) We synthesize insights about knowledge retention and prompt optimization in PLMs, analyze obstacles to adopting PLMs as knowledge bases and outline directions for future work.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility: A Representational Analysis of Content Effects
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concepts of validity and plausibility, and why do they conflate them, leading to content effects in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that validity and plausibility are linearly represented and aligned in LLMs, causing content effects, and that steering vectors can disentangle these concepts to reduce bias and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The representational entanglement of validity and plausibility in LLMs leads to content effects, and representational interventions offer a way to mitigate these biases for more logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit content effects where plausibility influences validity judgments, especially in zero-shot settings.
Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded as single directions in the model's activation space, and these vectors are highly similar.
The degree of alignment between validity and plausibility vectors predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models.
Plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgments, and vice versa, demonstrating cross-concept influence.
Debiasing steering vectors that disentangle validity from plausibility can reduce content effects and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.abstract: Both humans and large language models (LLMs) exhibit content effects: biases in which the plausibility of the semantic content of a reasoning problem influences judgments regarding its logical validity. While this phenomenon in humans is best explained by the dual-process theory of reasoning, the mechanisms behind content effects in LLMs remain unclear. In this work, we address this issue by investigating how LLMs encode the concepts of validity and plausibility within their internal representations. We show that both concepts are linearly represented and strongly aligned in representational geometry, leading models to conflate plausibility with validity. Using steering vectors, we demonstrate that plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgements, and vice versa, and that the degree of alignment between these two concepts predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models. Finally, we construct debiasing vectors that disentangle these concepts, reducing content effects and improving reasoning accuracy. Our findings advance understanding of how abstract logical concepts are represented in LLMs and highlight representational interventions as a path toward more logical systems.

papers.title: Unveiling LLMs: The Evolution of Latent Representations in a Dynamic Knowledge Graph
papers.research_question: Which factual knowledge do LLMs use to assess input truthfulness? How does this knowledge evolve across layers? Are there any distinctive patterns in its evolution?
papers.core_contribution: An end-to-end framework that decodes factual knowledge from LLM latent representations (as ground predicates) and represents its layer-wise evolution as a dynamic knowledge graph, enabling local and global interpretability analyses.
papers.conclusion: By decoding semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this framework advances our understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process and the mechanistic interpretability of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Entity centrality is highlighted in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluations.
The global analysis reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts.
Early layers focus on syntax and entity resolution, while middle layers are crucial for factual knowledge resolution.
The framework can identify representation errors, such as entity confusion, duplication, and example leakage, that lead to incorrect evaluations.
The model's classification performance shows an imbalance, with higher precision for true claims and higher recall for false claims on FEVER, and more balanced recall on CLIMATE-FEVER.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive capacity to recall a vast range of factual knowledge. However, understanding their underlying reasoning and internal mechanisms in exploiting this knowledge remains a key research area. This work unveils the factual information an LLM represents internally for sentence-level claim verification. We propose an end-to-end framework to decode factual knowledge embedded in token representations from a vector space to a set of ground predicates, showing its layer-wise evolution using a dynamic knowledge graph. Our framework employs activation patching, a vector-level technique that alters a token representation during inference, to extract encoded knowledge. Accordingly, we neither rely on training nor external models. Using factual and common-sense claims from two claim verification datasets, we showcase interpretability analyses at local and global levels. The local analysis highlights entity centrality in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluation. On the other hand, the global reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts. By interpreting semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this work enhances the understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for final predictions in large language models, specifically for knowledge storage?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static neuron-level attribution method based on log probability increase that outperforms other static methods, and uses it to analyze knowledge storage in attention and FFN layers of LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate 'query neurons', with analysis on six knowledge types helping to understand LLM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed log probability increase method for neuron attribution achieves superior performance compared to seven other static methods across three metrics (MRR, probability, log probability).
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics (e.g., language, country, city) tends to be stored in the same heads, while knowledge with distinct semantics is stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction, despite many neurons contributing.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which in turn are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B; comparing knowledge storage across different models is essential.
Uses static methods for attribution; comparing with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods is important.
future_direction: Explore other types of knowledge beyond the six studied.
Compare knowledge storage similarities and differences across different models.
Compare static attribution methods with other methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Understanding Gated Neurons in Transformers from Their Input-Output Functionality
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between what a neuron reads and what it writes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parameter-based method to classify gated neurons in transformers by input-output weight similarity, finding that enrichment neurons dominate early-middle layers while depletion neurons are more common in later layers.
papers.conclusion: The input-output perspective complements activation-dependent analyses and approaches that treat input and output separately, providing insights into how neurons manipulate concepts in the residual stream.
papers.key_findings:
Enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers across all 12 models studied, whereas later layers tend more towards depletion neurons.
A large proportion of neurons are input manipulators, with conditional enrichment being the most common class, especially in early-middle layers.
Many neurons exhibit double checking, where gate and input weight vectors are approximately orthogonal but intuitively represent the same concept.
The median cosine similarity between input and output weights is positive in early layers and negative in later layers, indicating a smooth transition in functionality.
Neurons rarely have prototypical weight configurations; instead, they often add novel but related information to the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method is parameter-based and therefore limited in scope; it is not designed to replace other neuron analysis methods.
Mathematical similarities of weights may not reflect semantic similarity; orthogonal vectors can represent similar concepts, and similar vectors can represent non-identical concepts.
Case studies of individual neurons may be cherry-picked, focusing on interpretable neurons in later layers, so interpretations may not generalize.
The paper provides only possible interpretations of observed phenomena, not definitive explanations.
future_direction: Extend the method to non-gated activation functions.
Study the evolution of input-output functionalities during model training.
Go beyond the analysis of single neurons to understand how neurons work together within and across classes.
papers.abstract: Interpretability researchers have attempted to understand MLP neurons of language models based on both the contexts in which they activate and their output weight vectors. They have paid little attention to a complementary aspect: the interactions between input and output. For example, when neurons detect a direction in the input, they might add much the same direction to the residual stream ("enrichment neurons") or reduce its presence ("depletion neurons"). We address this aspect by examining the cosine similarity between input and output weights of a neuron. We apply our method to 12 models and find that enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers whereas later layers tend more towards depletion. To explain this finding, we argue that enrichment neurons are largely responsible for enriching concept representations, one of the first steps of factual recall. Our input-output perspective is a complement to activation-dependent analyses and to approaches that treat input and output separately.

papers.title: Understanding Factual Recall in Transformers via Associative Memories
papers.research_question: How do transformers store factual information and what is their storage capacity?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow transformers can achieve near-optimal storage capacity for factual recall by using associative memories in both self-attention and MLP components, with a trade-off between them.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can efficiently store factual information using associative memories implemented in self-attention and MLP components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear and MLP associative memories can store a number of associations proportional to their parameter count.
A one-layer transformer can achieve 100% accuracy on a synthetic factual recall task when either the total self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scale linearly with the number of facts.
The transformer exhibits sequential learning dynamics during training, with an initial 'hallucination' stage.
The storage constructions are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
papers.limitation: The linear associative memory construction requires the association function to be injective for optimal capacity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated an impressive ability to perform factual recall. Prior work has found that transformers trained on factual recall tasks can store information at a rate proportional to their parameter count. In our work, we show that shallow transformers can use a combination of associative memories to obtain such near optimal storage capacity. We begin by proving that the storage capacities of both linear and MLP associative memories scale linearly with parameter count. We next introduce a synthetic factual recall task, and prove that a transformer with a single layer of self-attention followed by an MLP can obtain 100% accuracy on the task whenever either the total number of self-attention parameters or MLP parameters scales (up to log factors) linearly with the number of facts. In particular, the transformer can trade off between using the value matrices or the MLP as an associative memory to store the dataset of facts. We complement these expressivity results with an analysis of the gradient flow trajectory of a simplified linear attention model trained on our factual recall task, where we show that the model exhibits sequential learning behavior.

papers.title: Gradient Localization Improves Lifelong Pretraining of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can gradient localization be used to improve continual pretraining of language models for temporal knowledge updates and reduce catastrophic forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Traced Gradient Layers (TGL), a method that uses gradient norms to identify and target specific layers during continual pretraining, improving knowledge uptake and reducing forgetting.
papers.conclusion: The proposed TGL method improves continual pretraining by localizing gradient updates to relevant layers, as demonstrated on knowledge probing tasks without requiring fine-grained annotations.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient norms for knowledge-intensive salient spans are significantly higher in specific layers compared to standard pretraining.
Targeting updates to layers with high relative gradient norms improves performance on temporal knowledge probing tasks.
TGL methods can be applied on top of existing continual learning techniques to enhance their effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
It is unclear whether improvements in knowledge probe perplexity transfer to downstream settings.
Reductions in pretraining cost may lead to increased model pretraining due to Jevons Paradox.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on web-scale text corpora have been shown to capture world knowledge in their parameters. However, the mechanism by which language models store different types of knowledge is poorly understood. In this work, we examine two types of knowledge relating to temporally sensitive entities and demonstrate that each type is localized to different sets of parameters within the LLMs. We hypothesize that the lack of consideration of the locality of knowledge in existing continual learning methods contributes to both: the failed uptake of new information, and catastrophic forgetting of previously learned information. We observe that sequences containing references to updated and newly mentioned entities exhibit larger gradient norms in a subset of layers. We demonstrate that targeting parameter updates to these relevant layers can improve the performance of continually pretraining on language containing temporal drift.

papers.title: Precise Localization of Memories: A Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing Technique for LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we improve the locality of knowledge editing in LLMs by moving from causal tracing to neuron-level localization?
papers.core_contribution: FiNE is a neuron-level knowledge editing method that improves editing locality by precisely identifying and modifying neurons in FFNs, overcoming the over-reliance on subject entities in previous causal tracing methods.
papers.conclusion: FiNE advances knowledge localization and editing in LLMs by providing a neuron-level approach that improves locality and efficiency, paving the way for more reliable knowledge management.
papers.key_findings:
Existing locate-then-edit methods based on causal tracing are overly subject-driven and neglect relations, leading to poor editing locality.
FiNE's neuron-level localization provides more precise knowledge localization than causal tracing.
FiNE achieves better locality scores and efficiency compared to existing methods like ROME, MEMIT, and PMET.
FiNE maintains high edit success and portability while significantly improving locality.
Ablation studies show that neuron localization and layer freezing are important components of FiNE.
papers.limitation: The safety of edits cannot be ensured, and there is potential for misuse such as introducing malicious misinformation or bias.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated information in Large Language Models (LLMs). A representative line of study is locate-then-edit methods, which typically employ causal tracing to identify the modules responsible for recalling factual knowledge about entities. However, we find these methods are often sensitive only to changes in the subject entity, leaving them less effective at adapting to changes in relations. This limitation results in poor editing locality, which can lead to the persistence of irrelevant or inaccurate facts, ultimately compromising the reliability of LLMs. We believe this issue arises from the insufficient precision of knowledge localization. To address this, we propose a Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing (FiNE) method that enhances editing locality without affecting overall success rates. By precisely identifying and modifying specific neurons within feed-forward networks, FiNE significantly improves knowledge localization and editing. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that FiNE efficiently achieves better overall performance compared to existing techniques, providing new insights into the localization and modification of knowledge within LLMs.

papers.title: On Linear Representations and Pretraining Data Frequency in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the connection between pretraining data frequency and the formation of linear representations of factual relations in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The formation of linear representations for factual recall in language models is strongly correlated with pretraining term frequencies, and measuring these representations allows prediction of term frequencies in the pretraining corpus.
papers.conclusion: Linear representations of factual triplets in LMs are connected to pretraining frequencies, which can guide interpretability work and enable prediction of term frequencies in closed-data models.
papers.key_findings:
The development of linear representations for factual recall relations in LMs is related to frequency as well as model size.
Linear representations form at predictable frequency thresholds during training, regardless of when this threshold is met, and correlate strongly with recall accuracy.
Measuring the extent to which a relation is represented linearly allows prediction of the approximate frequencies of individual terms in the pretraining corpus, even without access to the training data.
The predictive signal from linear representations is stronger than that from log probabilities and task accuracies alone.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on factual relations and leaves non-factual relations (e.g., gender stereotypes) for future work.
The regression model provides approximate frequency predictions within bounds, not exact counts.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to non-factual relations.
Improve the bounds of predicted frequencies.
Understand if and when LMs use non-linear methods to solve tasks.
papers.abstract: Pretraining data has a direct impact on the behaviors and quality of language models (LMs), but we only understand the most basic principles of this relationship. While most work focuses on pretraining data's effect on downstream task behavior, we investigate its relationship to LM representations. Previous work has discovered that, in language models, some concepts are encoded `linearly' in the representations, but what factors cause these representations to form? We study the connection between pretraining data frequency and models' linear representations of factual relations. We find evidence that the formation of linear representations is strongly connected to pretraining term frequencies; specifically for subject-relation-object fact triplets, both subject-object co-occurrence frequency and in-context learning accuracy for the relation are highly correlated with linear representations. This is the case across all phases of pretraining. In OLMo-7B and GPT-J, we discover that a linear representation consistently (but not exclusively) forms when the subjects and objects within a relation co-occur at least 1k and 2k times, respectively, regardless of when these occurrences happen during pretraining. Finally, we train a regression model on measurements of linear representation quality in fully-trained LMs that can predict how often a term was seen in pretraining. Our model achieves low error even on inputs from a different model with a different pretraining dataset, providing a new method for estimating properties of the otherwise-unknown training data of closed-data models. We conclude that the strength of linear representations in LMs contains signal about the models' pretraining corpora that may provide new avenues for controlling and improving model behavior: particularly, manipulating the models' training data to meet specific frequency thresholds.

papers.title: Filtering with Self-Attention and Storing with MLP: One-Layer Transformers Can Provably Acquire and Extract Knowledge
papers.research_question: How do transformers acquire knowledge during pre-training via next-token prediction and extract it after fine-tuning? Under what conditions can pre-trained transformers perform out-of-distribution generalization after full and low-rank fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a theoretical framework for one-layer transformers that shows they can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss and post-fine-tuning out-of-distribution generalization under certain conditions, and explains the roles of self-attention and MLP in knowledge acquisition and extraction.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework provides convergence and generalization guarantees for one-layer transformers, elucidating the mechanisms of knowledge acquisition and extraction and the conditions for successful out-of-distribution generalization after fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can achieve near-optimal pre-training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition.
Given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction.
Violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations.
Self-attention learns to filter out noise tokens and focus on subject and relation tokens, enabling the MLP to learn balanced features for subjects and relations.
Low-rank fine-tuning is effective because the fine-tuning gradients closely approximate their best rank-1 form, with the right singular vector aligning with the Q&A format embedding.
papers.limitation: Uses orthogonal embeddings and simplified architecture, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Analysis of random embeddings instead of orthogonal embeddings.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on knowledge-intensive tasks, yet the theoretical mechanisms underlying knowledge acquisition (storage and memorization) during pre-training and extraction (retrieval and recall) during inference after fine-tuning remain poorly understood. Although prior theoretical studies have explored these processes through analyses of training dynamics, they overlook critical components essential for a comprehensive theory: (1) the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), empirically identified as the primary module for knowledge storage; (2) out-of-distribution (OOD) adaptivity, which enables LLMs to generalize to unseen scenarios post-pre-training; and (3) next-token prediction, the standard autoregressive objective that encodes knowledge as conditional probabilities. In this work, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical framework that addresses these limitations by examining the training dynamics of one-layer transformers. Under regularity assumptions, we establish that: (i) transformers attain near-optimal training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition; (ii) given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction; and (iii) violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations. Our analysis encompasses both full fine-tuning and low-rank fine-tuning, yielding insights into the efficacy of practical low-rank adaptation methods. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic datasets and the real-world PopQA benchmark, employing GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B models.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others.
