The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: On Relation-Specific Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do relation-specific neurons exist in large language models, i.e., neurons that focus on a relation itself independent of any entity, and what are their properties?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates the existence of relation-specific neurons in LLMs and provides evidence for their properties: cumulativity, versatility, and interference.
papers.conclusion: Relation-specific neurons exist in LLMs and exhibit properties of cumulativity, versatility, and interference, indicating distributed and overlapping encoding of relational knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Relation-specific neurons exist in LLMs and are located primarily in the middle layers.
Neuron cumulativity: Multiple neurons jointly contribute to processing facts involving a relation, with no single neuron fully encoding a fact.
Neuron versatility: Neurons can be shared across multiple closely related as well as less related relations, and some transfer across languages.
Neuron interference: Deactivating neurons specific to one relation can improve LLMs' factual recall performance for facts of other relations.
The effect of deactivating relation-specific neurons is more pronounced when more neurons are deactivated, and the neurons are effective across different prompt templates and languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a set of 12 relations and two model families (LLama-2 and Gemma).
future_direction: Extend analysis to more relations and model families.
Investigate the dynamics of relation-specific neurons during training.
Explore whether similar neurons exist for other types of knowledge or tasks.
papers.abstract: In large language models (LLMs), certain \emph{neurons} can store distinct pieces of knowledge learned during pretraining. While factual knowledge typically appears as a combination of \emph{relations} and \emph{entities}, it remains unclear whether some neurons focus on a relation itself -- independent of any entity. We hypothesize such neurons \emph{detect} a relation in the input text and \emph{guide} generation involving such a relation. To investigate this, we study the LLama-2 family on a chosen set of relations, with a \textit{statistics}-based method. Our experiments demonstrate the existence of relation-specific neurons. We measure the effect of selectively deactivating candidate neurons specific to relation $r$ on the LLM's ability to handle (1) facts involving relation $r$ and (2) facts involving a different relation $r' \neq r$. With respect to their capacity for encoding relation information, we give evidence for the following three properties of relation-specific neurons. \textbf{(i) Neuron cumulativity.} Multiple neurons jointly contribute to processing facts involving relation $r$, with no single neuron fully encoding a fact in $r$ on its own. \textbf{(ii) Neuron versatility.} Neurons can be shared across multiple closely related as well as less related relations. In addition, some relation neurons transfer across languages. \textbf{(iii) Neuron interference.} Deactivating neurons specific to one relation can improve LLMs' factual recall performance for facts of other relations. We make our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/cisnlp/relation-specific-neurons.

papers.title: Facts in Stats: Impacts of Pretraining Diversity on Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: How does the diversity of pretraining data (in terms of contextual variation) impact the generalization of language models in learning both statistical patterns and factual associations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a synthetic testbed to study how pretraining diversity affects generalization, finding that diversity impacts in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance differently depending on contextual structure, and identifies optimization bottlenecks in embedding and unembedding layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, the synthetic framework allows isolation of effects that would be confounded in large-scale studies, offering a controlled testbed for future investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Higher diversity can slow in-distribution factual recall while leaving in-distribution statistical accuracy largely unaffected.
Out-of-distribution effects depend on contextual structure: low diversity can severely impact factual recall, statistical accuracy, or both.
Data diversity introduces a cost-benefit dynamic: with limited training time, intermediate diversity levels are optimal.
The learning dynamics of the statistical and factual streams are coupled: increased complexity in one stream delays learning of both.
Through targeted interventions, optimization bottlenecks for out-of-distribution generalization are localized to the embedding and unembedding layers.
future_direction: Characterizing how context diversity and model capacity reshape the in-distribution loss landscape
papers.abstract: Language models are pretrained on sequences that blend statistical regularities (making text fluent) with factual associations between specific tokens (knowledge of facts). While recent work suggests that the variability of their interaction, such as paraphrases of factual associations, critically determines generalization ability, we lack a systematic analysis of these impacts. This paper introduces a flexible synthetic testbed that combines a statistical stream of generic tokens with an abstract factual stream of source-target token pairs, enabling fine-grained control over their interaction. The design enables the independent control of diversity nature by manipulating stream composition (contextual structure) and the diversity level by varying which statistical streams each fact appears in. Through controlled experiments, we find that while higher contextual diversity delays in-distribution (ID) factual accuracy, its impact on out-of-distribution (OOD) factual generalization depends critically on contextual structure. In some cases, OOD performance follows the same trend as ID, but in others, diversity becomes essential for non-trivial factual recall. Even when low diversity prohibits factual recall, optimal diversity levels depend on training duration. Beyond factual recall failures, we identify structures where statistical generalization fails independently, and others where both capabilities degrade. This shows how the interplay between contextual design and diversity level impacts different generalization aspects. Further, through a series of controlled interventions on the model components, we trace the OOD failures to distinct optimization bottlenecks, highlighting the importance of the embedding and unembedding layers. Our synthetic framework allows us to isolate effects that would be confounded in large-scale studies, offering a controlled testbed for future investigations.

papers.title: Discovering Salient Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify subsets of neurons that learn specific linguistic properties, and how is linguistic knowledge localized, distributed, and affected by fine-tuning in NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) for extracting salient neurons in NLP models, revealing that linguistic knowledge is localized in lower layers for basic properties and distributed in higher layers for complex concepts, with variations across models and during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The LCA method provides insights into how linguistic knowledge is encoded in neurons, showing localization patterns and redistribution during fine-tuning, with implications for model understanding and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Small subsets of neurons can predict different linguistic tasks.
Neurons for basic lexical information are localized in lower layers, while those for complex concepts are in higher layers.
Linguistic information is redundantly preserved across neurons.
During transfer learning, salient linguistic neurons relocate to lower layers in some models like RoBERTa and XLNet.
Multilingual models exhibit similar neuron distribution for concepts across different languages.
future_direction: Pinpointing specific concepts regressed to lower layers versus those retained in higher layers during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: While a lot of work has been done in understanding representations learned within deep NLP models and what knowledge they capture, little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We present a technique called as Linguistic Correlation Analysis to extract salient neurons in the model, with respect to any extrinsic property - with the goal of understanding how such a knowledge is preserved within neurons. We carry out a fine-grained analysis to answer the following questions: (i) can we identify subsets of neurons in the network that capture specific linguistic properties? (ii) how localized or distributed neurons are across the network? iii) how redundantly is the information preserved? iv) how fine-tuning pre-trained models towards downstream NLP tasks, impacts the learned linguistic knowledge? iv) how do architectures vary in learning different linguistic properties? Our data-driven, quantitative analysis illuminates interesting findings: (i) we found small subsets of neurons that can predict different linguistic tasks, ii) with neurons capturing basic lexical information (such as suffixation) localized in lower most layers, iii) while those learning complex concepts (such as syntactic role) predominantly in middle and higher layers, iii) that salient linguistic neurons are relocated from higher to lower layers during transfer learning, as the network preserve the higher layers for task specific information, iv) we found interesting differences across pre-trained models, with respect to how linguistic information is preserved within, and v) we found that concept exhibit similar neuron distribution across different languages in the multilingual transformer models. Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit.

papers.title: Balancing Knowledge Updates: Toward Unified Modular Editing in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in LLMs be improved by jointly updating both MLP and Attention modules, rather than focusing solely on MLP modules?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces IntAttn-Edit, a novel knowledge editing method that jointly updates both MLP and Attention modules using a knowledge balancing strategy, which proportionally allocates update magnitudes based on each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: IntAttn-Edit addresses the limitation of knowledge residuals in existing methods by jointly editing MLP and Attention modules, leading to more balanced and comprehensive knowledge updates that outperform existing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers, functioning as key-value associative memory structures.
IntAttn-Edit consistently outperforms existing editing baselines (e.g., ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit) on benchmarks like ZsRE and WikiData counterfact, achieving higher edit success and portability.
The proposed knowledge balancing strategy, which dynamically allocates update magnitudes between MLP and Attn modules based on their causal contributions, maintains editing performance within an optimal range.
Updating only a subset of knowledge-storage modules (e.g., only MLP) can leave residual outdated knowledge, which IntAttn-Edit mitigates by jointly editing both modules.
Extensive experiments show IntAttn-Edit delivers superior results across different batch sizes and models while maintaining high locality and fluency.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as an efficient approach for updating factual knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It typically locates knowledge storage modules and then modifies their parameters. However, most existing methods focus on the weights of multilayer perceptron (MLP) modules, which are often identified as the main repositories of factual information. Other components, such as attention (Attn) modules, are often ignored during editing. This imbalance can leave residual outdated knowledge and limit editing effectiveness. We perform comprehensive knowledge localization experiments on advanced LLMs and find that Attn modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers. Based on these insights, we propose IntAttn-Edit, a method that extends the associative memory paradigm to jointly update both MLP and Attn modules. Our approach uses a knowledge balancing strategy that allocates update magnitudes in proportion to each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that IntAttn-Edit achieves higher edit success, better generalization, and stronger knowledge preservation than prior methods. Further analysis shows that the balancing strategy keeps editing performance within an optimal range across diverse settings.

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them. We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: Revealing the Parametric Knowledge of Language Models: A Unified Framework for Attribution Methods
papers.research_question: What are the differences and complementary insights between instance attribution and neuron attribution methods in revealing the parametric knowledge of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified evaluation framework to compare instance and neuron attribution methods, showing that NA reveals more diverse knowledge while IA provides unique insights, suggesting a synergistic approach for holistic understanding.
papers.conclusion: IA and NA provide different explanations for parametric knowledge, suggesting a combined approach for holistic understanding. Neurons in MLP layers are insufficient, indicating attention weights also play a crucial role.
papers.key_findings:
NA-Instances discovers more diverse training instances than IA methods.
Neurons in MLP layers are not sufficient nor comprehensive for explaining predictions, indicating importance of attention layers.
Fine-tuning with influential instances from IA does not outperform random selection.
NA-Instances performs better at discovering dataset artifacts than IA methods.
IA and NA results have small overlap, suggesting complementary insights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments limited to two instance attribution methods, one neuron attribution method, three tasks, three language models, and English text only.
Computational restrictions prevented studying very large language models.
Only neurons in MLP layers were studied, not attention heads, so the interplay between MLP and attention is not captured.
future_direction: Investigate other NLP tasks and more language models, including very large ones and cross-lingual scenarios.
Study the interplay between MLP neurons and attention heads for a more complete understanding.
Further study the purpose of attribution methods, e.g., for dataset artifact detection.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) acquire parametric knowledge from their training process, embedding it within their weights. The increasing scalability of LMs, however, poses significant challenges for understanding a model's inner workings and further for updating or correcting this embedded knowledge without the significant cost of retraining. This underscores the importance of unveiling exactly what knowledge is stored and its association with specific model components. Instance Attribution (IA) and Neuron Attribution (NA) offer insights into this training-acquired knowledge, though they have not been compared systematically. Our study introduces a novel evaluation framework to quantify and compare the knowledge revealed by IA and NA. To align the results of the methods we introduce the attribution method NA-Instances to apply NA for retrieving influential training instances, and IA-Neurons to discover important neurons of influential instances discovered by IA. We further propose a comprehensive list of faithfulness tests to evaluate the comprehensiveness and sufficiency of the explanations provided by both methods. Through extensive experiments and analysis, we demonstrate that NA generally reveals more diverse and comprehensive information regarding the LM's parametric knowledge compared to IA. Nevertheless, IA provides unique and valuable insights into the LM's parametric knowledge, which are not revealed by NA. Our findings further suggest the potential of a synergistic approach of combining the diverse findings of IA and NA for a more holistic understanding of an LM's parametric knowledge.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Language Representation Projection: Can We Transfer Factual Knowledge across Languages in Multilingual Language Models?
papers.research_question: Can cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enable factual knowledge transfer across languages? Specifically, can we transfer factual knowledge from English to non-English languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes LRP2, a parameter-free method that projects representations between languages to align representation spaces, which improves factual knowledge retrieval and transfer across languages in multilingual language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper confirms that cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enables factual knowledge transfer across languages, and proposes LRP2 as an effective method for this transfer.
papers.key_findings:
LRP2 improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and cross-lingual transferability for non-English languages.
LRP2 aligns representation spaces: LIRP projects non-English representations to English-like ones, and LSRP projects them back to the non-English space.
LRP2 increases the overlap of knowledge neurons between English and non-English languages, indicating enhanced cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
Cross-lingual knowledge neurons exist in multilingual pretrained language models.
Different languages require different optimal layer configurations for the LIRP and LSRP modules, indicating varying degrees of representation alignment needed.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of LRP2 heavily relies on the inherent capabilities of multilingual pretrained language models.
Experiments are limited to two relatively small models due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Investigate LRP2 on larger language models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models serve as repositories of multilingual factual knowledge. Nevertheless, a substantial performance gap of factual knowledge probing exists between high-resource languages and low-resource languages, suggesting limited implicit factual knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual pretrained language models. This paper investigates the feasibility of explicitly transferring relatively rich factual knowledge from English to non-English languages. To accomplish this, we propose two parameter-free Language Representation Projection modules (LRP2). The first module converts non-English representations into English-like equivalents, while the second module reverts English-like representations back into representations of the corresponding non-English language. Experimental results on the mLAMA dataset demonstrate that LRP2 significantly improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and facilitates knowledge transferability across diverse non-English languages. We further investigate the working mechanism of LRP2 from the perspectives of representation space and cross-lingual knowledge neuron.

papers.title: Retentive or Forgetful? Diving into the Knowledge Memorizing Mechanism of Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the memorizing dynamics of language models, and how does pre-training affect their memory ability?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-training transforms language models from forgetful to retentive by enabling long-term memory formation, influenced by knowledge relevance and diversity.
papers.conclusion: Vanilla language models are forgetful, pre-training leads to retentive models, and knowledge relevance and diversification significantly influence memory formation.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla language models are forgetful with short memory duration and limited capacity.
Pre-trained language models are retentive and can gradually memorize knowledge through repetitive learning.
Pre-training is crucial for developing long-term memory ability in language models.
There is memory competition between highly relevant knowledge types in pre-trained models.
Lack of knowledge diversity causes memory collapse in early learning stages.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying reasons for the forgetful-retentive transition during pre-training.
Explore other critical factors affecting memorization beyond pre-training and diversity.
Compare memorization mechanisms between language models and the human brain.
papers.abstract: Memory is one of the most essential cognitive functions serving as a repository of world knowledge and episodes of activities. In recent years, large-scale pre-trained language models have shown remarkable memorizing ability. On the contrary, vanilla neural networks without pre-training have been long observed suffering from the catastrophic forgetting problem. To investigate such a retentive-forgetful contradiction and understand the memory mechanism of language models, we conduct thorough experiments by controlling the target knowledge types, the learning strategies and the learning schedules. We find that: 1) Vanilla language models are forgetful; 2) Pre-training leads to retentive language models; 3) Knowledge relevance and diversification significantly influence the memory formation. These conclusions are useful for understanding the abilities of pre-trained language models and shed light on designing and evaluating new learning and inference algorithms of language models.

papers.title: Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent and track characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a pervasive 'lookback mechanism' that language models use to track characters' beliefs, and introduces the CausalToM dataset for causal analysis of Theory of Mind.
papers.conclusion: The lookback mechanism is a foundational computation for belief tracking in language models, providing a step toward reverse-engineering Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Language models use a systematic 'lookback mechanism' for belief tracking, which involves recalling important information when needed.
The mechanism uses Ordering IDs (OIs) to bind character-object-state triples in the residual stream of state tokens.
Three key lookbacks are identified: binding lookback (retrieves state OI), answer lookback (retrieves state token), and visibility lookback (updates beliefs based on visibility).
The mechanism generalizes across model scales (70B to 405B) and model families (Llama and Qwen).
The visibility lookback uses a visibility ID to retrieve information about observed characters and update the observing character's beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The visibility lookback mechanism is only partially understood and requires further investigation.
The mechanism does not scale to three characters in the visibility condition.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex scenarios with more characters and objects.
Further investigation of the visibility lookback mechanism.
Applying the lookback mechanism analysis to other tasks and domains.
papers.abstract: How do language models (LMs) represent characters' beliefs, especially when those beliefs may differ from reality? This question lies at the heart of understanding the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LMs. We analyze LMs' ability to reason about characters' beliefs using causal mediation and abstraction. We construct a dataset, CausalToM, consisting of simple stories where two characters independently change the state of two objects, potentially unaware of each other's actions. Our investigation uncovers a pervasive algorithmic pattern that we call a lookback mechanism, which enables the LM to recall important information when it becomes necessary. The LM binds each character-object-state triple together by co-locating their reference information, represented as Ordering IDs (OIs), in low-rank subspaces of the state token's residual stream. When asked about a character's beliefs regarding the state of an object, the binding lookback retrieves the correct state OI and then the answer lookback retrieves the corresponding state token. When we introduce text specifying that one character is (not) visible to the other, we find that the LM first generates a visibility ID encoding the relation between the observing and the observed character OIs. In a visibility lookback, this ID is used to retrieve information about the observed character and update the observing character's beliefs. Our work provides insights into belief tracking mechanisms, taking a step toward reverse-engineering ToM reasoning in LMs.

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: From RAGs to rich parameters: Probing how language models utilize external knowledge over parametric information for factual queries
papers.research_question: How do language models utilize external knowledge from RAG over parametric information for factual queries?
papers.core_contribution: Language models exhibit a shortcut behavior, minimally using parametric memory and relying more on external RAG context for factual queries.
papers.conclusion: In RAG settings, language models prioritize external context over internal parametric knowledge, reducing reliance on subject tokens and MLP activations.
papers.key_findings:
Language models minimally use parametric memory in MLPs when RAG context is present.
The last token residual stream is enriched from context attribute tokens rather than query subject tokens.
Attention contributions from subject tokens decrease with RAG, while attribute token contributions are higher.
Knocking out attention from subject tokens has minimal effect in RAG setting compared to vanilla.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to short RAG contexts due to computational overhead.
Context is synthetically generated and controlled, which may not reflect noisy real-world retrievals.
future_direction: Study the impact of long context and position biases like recency bias.
Analyze instruction-tuned and RLHF-finetuned models.
Examine noisy and real-world RAG outputs.
papers.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) enriches the ability of language models to reason using external context to augment responses for a given user prompt. This approach has risen in popularity due to practical applications in various applications of language models in search, question/answering, and chat-bots. However, the exact nature of how this approach works isn't clearly understood. In this paper, we mechanistically examine the RAG pipeline to highlight that language models take shortcut and have a strong bias towards utilizing only the context information to answer the question, while relying minimally on their parametric memory. We probe this mechanistic behavior in language models with: (i) Causal Mediation Analysis to show that the parametric memory is minimally utilized when answering a question and (ii) Attention Contributions and Knockouts to show that the last token residual stream do not get enriched from the subject token in the question, but gets enriched from other informative tokens in the context. We find this pronounced shortcut behaviour true across both LLaMa and Phi family of models.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: How do language models internally handle and recall temporally changing facts? Specifically, where within the model architecture does the mechanism for time-specific knowledge reside?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that mediate the recall of time-specific knowledge in LLMs. Ablating these heads degrades temporal fact recall while leaving time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance unaffected, and their activations can be used for temporal knowledge editing.
papers.conclusion: The work systematically uncovers Temporal Heads that selectively mediate time-variant knowledge in LLMs. These heads are causally important for temporal recall, can be activated by both numeric and textual time references, and offer a target for precise temporal knowledge editing without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specific attention heads (Temporal Heads) are identified across multiple models (e.g., a15.h0, a18.h3 in Llama2) that are crucial for recalling time-specific facts.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal impact on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated not only by numeric time conditions (e.g., 'In 2004') but also by textual aliases (e.g., 'In the year the Summer Olympics were held in Athens'), indicating they encode a broader temporal dimension.
The importance of Temporal Heads varies across different years and knowledge categories, with stronger effects around periods of factual transition.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by selectively adjusting the activation values of these heads, demonstrating their role as a key component for modifying time-sensitive information.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs like General ChroKnowledge was constrained, as the underlying multiple-choice options typically do not exhibit temporal dependencies.
The circuit analysis method (EAP-IG) did not support models with Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), excluding models like Llama-3-8B-Instruct from the main analysis.
future_direction: Future work should include broader application of the findings for enhancing temporal reasoning to increase practical value.

papers.title: Finding Experts in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: What is the presence of expert units in pre-trained Transformer Models, and how do they impact model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify expert units in transformer models, shows that the presence of these experts correlates with model generalization, and demonstrates how to use them for model evaluation and conditioned text generation without additional training.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that expert units are valuable for understanding, evaluating, and controlling transformer models, enabling applications like model ranking and concept-conditioned text generation.
papers.key_findings:
Expert units in transformer models are correlated with generalization power, with a squared Pearson correlation of 0.833.
Concepts with similar meanings share expert units, indicating co-learning, which can be used for explainability.
By forcing top expert units to be active, pre-trained language models can generate text containing specific concepts without fine-tuning.
Shallow layers in transformers acquire more concepts than deep layers, similar to observations in image GANs.
Homograph concepts are harder to disambiguate at the unit level compared to sense concepts.
papers.abstract: In this work we study the presence of expert units in pre-trained Transformer Models (TM), and how they impact a model's performance. We define expert units to be neurons that are able to classify a concept with a given average precision, where a concept is represented by a binary set of sentences containing the concept (or not). Leveraging the OneSec dataset (Scarlini et al., 2019), we compile a dataset of 1641 concepts that allows diverse expert units in TM to be discovered. We show that expert units are important in several ways: (1) The presence of expert units is correlated ($r^2=0.833$) with the generalization power of TM, which allows ranking TM without requiring fine-tuning on suites of downstream tasks. We further propose an empirical method to decide how accurate such experts should be to evaluate generalization. (2) The overlap of top experts between concepts provides a sensible way to quantify concept co-learning, which can be used for explainability of unknown concepts. (3) We show how to self-condition off-the-shelf pre-trained language models to generate text with a given concept by forcing the top experts to be active, without requiring re-training the model or using additional parameters.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models learn grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data? What does this consistency reveal about their inductive biases and linguistic representations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, indicating a shared inductive bias. The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional, meaning that overall performance predicts which linguistic generalizations have been acquired.
papers.conclusion: Studying learning trajectories is a promising approach to understand linguistic representations in NLMs, and the consistency suggests a mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2 and TransformerXL) also show similar learning trajectories when aligned by performance level.
The choice of training data has some effect but does not override the consistent ordering.
The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar performance on individual phenomena.
Early in training, NLMs rely on local cues and resemble bag-of-words models; later they become more sensitive to structural cues.
future_direction: Consider the impact of additional factors, architectures and learning phases that appear only later in training.
Develop a theory that can account for the patterns presented by NLMs’ learning trajectories.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: Continual Memorization of Factoids in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models forget factoids in continual fine-tuning, and can data mixing strategies mitigate this forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the continual memorization setting to study forgetting of factoids in language models, and proposes REMIX, a data mixing strategy that effectively mitigates forgetting.
papers.conclusion: REMIX effectively mitigates forgetting in continual memorization by diversifying and shifting factoid storage to earlier layers, revealing patterns of robust memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Forgetting is most severe when the second stage of training involves another factoid dataset.
Replay methods are insufficient to prevent forgetting in this setting.
Mixing random word sequences or generic pretraining data (REMIX) effectively mitigates forgetting.
REMIX causes factoids to be stored in earlier layers and diversifies storage across layers.
REMIX enables better knowledge manipulation compared to no mixing.
papers.limitation: Knowledge manipulation remains extremely hard for fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: As new knowledge rapidly accumulates, language models (LMs) with pretrained knowledge quickly become obsolete. A common approach to updating LMs is fine-tuning them directly on new knowledge. However, recent studies have shown that fine-tuning for memorization may be ineffective in storing knowledge or may exacerbate hallucinations. In this work, we introduce a setting we call continual memorization, where a model must memorize and retain a set of factoids through multiple stages of fine-tuning on subsequent datasets. We characterized the forgetting patterns through extensive experiments and show that LMs widely suffer from forgetting, especially when needing to memorize factoids in the second stage. We posit that forgetting can be alleviated by modifying training dynamics: (1) protecting the memorization process when learning factoids or (2) reducing interference from subsequent training stages. Intriguingly, we find that mixing randomly generated word sequences or generic data sampled from pretraining corpora at different training stages effectively mitigates forgetting REMIX: Random and Generic Data Mixing). REMIX can recover performance from severe forgetting, outperforming replay methods and other continual learning baselines. We analyze how REMIX influences the learning process and find that robust memorization follows a distinct pattern: the model stores factoids in earlier layers than usual and diversifies the layers that retain them, which results in easier recall and manipulate of the learned factoids.

papers.title: Improving Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Can reasoning performance in LLMs be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning performance in LLMs can be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference, without any additional training.
papers.conclusion: The experiments indicate that reasoning can in part be understood to be encoded in the residual stream, similarly to how emotional valence or other features are encoded, and can be modulated via representation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Control vectors derived from contrastive pairs or PCA can improve model performance on inductive, deductive, and mathematical reasoning tasks.
The intervention generalizes across tasks: control vectors from bAbI improve GSM8K performance and vice versa.
The intervention changes the model's internal representations, as evidenced by changes in KL divergence and entropy.
The method requires no additional training and works by adding control vectors to the residual stream during inference.
The optimal scaling factor α varies across models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Limited scope of models (smaller than production-level state-of-the-art models).
The IOI task is relatively simple, which limits the scope of potential errors and the generalizability of findings.
The need for better contrastive pairs for reasoning to optimally derive control vectors.
future_direction: Applying the intervention to much larger models.
Applying the intervention to more general tasks.
Testing different contrastive schemes.
Exploring ways of embedding this methodology into the models.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have resulted in increasingly anthropomorphic language concerning the ability of LLMs to reason. Whether reasoning in LLMs should be understood to be inherently different is, however, widely debated. We propose utilizing a representation engineering approach wherein model activations are read from the residual stream of an LLM when processing a reasoning task. The activations are used to derive a control vector that is applied to the model as an inference-time intervention, modulating the representational space of the model, to improve performance on the specified task. We publish the code for deriving control vectors and analyzing model representations. The method allows us to improve performance on reasoning benchmarks and assess how control vectors influence the final logit distribution of a model via metrics such as KL divergence and entropy. We apply control vectors to Mistral-7B-Instruct and a range of Pythia models on an inductive, a deductive and mathematical reasoning task. We show that an LLM can, to a certain degree, be controlled to improve its perceived reasoning ability by modulating activations. The intervention is dependent upon the ability to reliably extract the model's typical state when correctly solving a task. Our results suggest that reasoning performance can be modulated in the same manner as other information-processing tasks performed by LLMs and demonstrate that we are capable of improving performance on specific tasks via a simple intervention on the residual stream with no additional training.

papers.title: Is Factuality Enhancement a Free Lunch For LLMs? Better Factuality Can Lead to Worse Context-Faithfulness
papers.research_question: Does enhancing factuality in LLMs lead to a decline in context-faithfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Factuality enhancement methods can improve factuality but significantly undermine context-faithfulness in LLMs, causing overconfidence in parametric knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Factuality enhancement methods pose risks to context-faithfulness, and future research should balance both factual accuracy and context adherence.
papers.key_findings:
Factuality enhancement methods lead to a significant decline in context-faithfulness, with editing accuracy dropping by up to 60.3%.
The probability of new knowledge tokens decreases while parametric knowledge tokens increase after applying factuality enhancement.
Hidden states become more aligned with parametric outputs after context injection.
future_direction: Explore strategies to balance factuality and context-faithfulness in LLMs.
papers.abstract: As the modern tools of choice for text understanding and generation, large language models (LLMs) are expected to accurately output answers by leveraging the input context. This requires LLMs to possess both context-faithfulness and factual accuracy. Extensive efforts have been made to enable better outputs from LLMs by mitigating hallucinations through factuality enhancement methods. However, they also pose risks of hindering context-faithfulness, as factuality enhancement can lead LLMs to become overly confident in their parametric knowledge, causing them to overlook the relevant input context. In this work, we argue that current factuality enhancement methods can significantly undermine the context-faithfulness of LLMs. We first revisit the current factuality enhancement methods and evaluate their effectiveness in enhancing factual accuracy. Next, we evaluate their performance on knowledge editing tasks to assess the potential impact on context-faithfulness. The experimental results reveal that while these methods may yield inconsistent improvements in factual accuracy, they also cause a more severe decline in context-faithfulness, with the largest decrease reaching a striking 69.7\%. To explain these declines, we analyze the hidden states and logit distributions for the tokens representing new knowledge and parametric knowledge respectively, highlighting the limitations of current approaches. Our finding highlights the complex trade-offs inherent in enhancing LLMs. Therefore, we recommend that more research on LLMs' factuality enhancement make efforts to reduce the sacrifice of context-faithfulness.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: One Mind, Many Tongues: A Deep Dive into Language-Agnostic Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons in large language models, considering uncertainty across queries and languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MATRICE, a method for localizing language-agnostic knowledge neurons by quantifying uncertainty across queries and languages, and constructs the RML-LAMA benchmark. It demonstrates these neurons' roles in cross-lingual editing, knowledge enhancement, and injection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed MATRICE method accurately localizes language-agnostic knowledge neurons, and these neurons are shown to be conducive to cross-lingual knowledge editing, enhancement, and injection.
papers.key_findings:
A significant proportion of language-agnostic knowledge neurons are distributed in the last few layers of LLMs.
Manipulating (suppressing/enhancing) language-agnostic knowledge neurons significantly affects knowledge expression across languages.
A single edit on language-agnostic knowledge neurons can simultaneously modify corresponding knowledge in all languages (cross-lingual editing).
Amplifying the activation of language-agnostic knowledge neurons improves prediction performance in low-resource languages.
Fine-tuning only parameters associated with language-agnostic knowledge neurons helps LLMs learn new knowledge while alleviating forgetting of old knowledge.
papers.limitation: The approach is based on knowledge neuron theory and focuses on factual knowledge, not yet extended to other types like commonsense or event knowledge.
future_direction: Extend the approach to investigate other types of knowledge, such as commonsense knowledge and event knowledge.
Adapt the method to new theoretical frameworks as the theory of knowledge neurons evolves.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have learned vast amounts of factual knowledge through self-supervised pre-training on large-scale corpora. Meanwhile, LLMs have also demonstrated excellent multilingual capabilities, which can express the learned knowledge in multiple languages. However, the knowledge storage mechanism in LLMs still remains mysterious. Some researchers attempt to demystify the factual knowledge in LLMs from the perspective of knowledge neurons, and subsequently discover language-agnostic knowledge neurons that store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language barriers. However, the preliminary finding suffers from two limitations: 1) High Uncertainty in Localization Results. Existing study only uses a prompt-based probe to localize knowledge neurons for each fact, while LLMs cannot provide consistent answers for semantically equivalent queries. Thus, it leads to inaccurate localization results with high uncertainty. 2) Lack of Analysis in More Languages. The study only analyzes language-agnostic knowledge neurons on English and Chinese data, without exploring more language families and languages. Naturally, it limits the generalizability of the findings. To address aforementioned problems, we first construct a new benchmark called Rephrased Multilingual LAMA (RML-LAMA), which contains high-quality cloze-style multilingual parallel queries for each fact.
